exercises.title: A new matrix: find dominance
exercises.prompt: This is a different game, not the Grade Game. Which statement is true for the row player?

options.text: Neither strategy strictly dominates the other.

exercises.explanation: If your partner chooses A: 2 > 0; if your partner chooses B: 4 > 3. So A strictly dominates B.

exercises.title: Dominance may be where you least expect it
exercises.prompt: Compare your payoffs in this matrix. Which strategy should you eliminate?

options.text: Eliminate A: it is strictly dominated by B.
Eliminate B: it is strictly dominated by A.
Neither: there is no strict dominance.

exercises.explanation: Against your partner’s A, B gives you 4 instead of 2; against their B, it gives you 1 instead of 0. Your strategy A is therefore strictly dominated.

exercises.title: The indignant angels model
exercises.prompt: Which of your strategies is strictly dominant in the indignant angels matrix?
exercises.explanation: Against α, α is better (0 > −3); against β, β is better (1 > −1). Neither strategy outperforms the other in every case.
exercises.context: In this model, both players care about their own grade and fairness. You choose the row; your partner chooses the column. The numbers are payoffs reflecting these preferences.

exercises.title: A better outcome is not enough
exercises.prompt: Why can’t you conclude “both should choose β” merely from seeing that (1,1) is better than (0,0)?

options.text: Because neither player controls the other’s choice, and if the partner chooses β, the incentive to deviate to α remains.
Because total payoffs never matter in game theory.
Because (0,0) is always the best outcome.

exercises.explanation: An improvement requiring both players to act does not follow from one player’s decision. If your partner plays β, your payoff from α is 3, compared with 1 from β.
exercises.context: You choose the row; your partner chooses the column. Both players care only about their own grade; the matrix shows their payoffs.

exercises.title: The other player’s preferences
exercises.prompt: First predict your partner’s choice, then find your best response. Both players are rational and know each other’s preferences.

options.text: You choose α, your partner chooses α.
You choose α, your partner chooses β.
You choose β, your partner chooses α.
You choose β, your partner chooses β.

exercises.explanation: For your partner, α strictly dominates β: if you choose α, they get 0 instead of −1; if you choose β, they get 3 instead of 1. So you expect α. Your best response is α: 0 > −3. Your α does not strictly dominate β, however: against your partner’s β, your β is better (1 > −1).
exercises.context: You are an indignant angel: you care about your own grade and fairness, and choose the row. Your partner cares only about their own grade and chooses the column. These are preference types in the model, not moral judgments.

exercises.title: Promises and commitments
exercises.prompt: In this game, two people promise to choose β. There is no penalty for breaking the promise. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: A promise need not change incentives if breaking it has no consequences.
Any spoken promise makes β a strictly dominant strategy.
Repeated games and commitments can never affect cooperation.

exercises.explanation: Communication alone does not change the original payoff matrix. Enforceable commitments and repeated interaction can create additional incentives.
exercises.context: You choose the row; your partner chooses the column. Both players care only about their own grade; the matrix shows their payoffs.

text.00: Each player prefers α regardless of the other’s choice; both end up with 0.
text.11: Both would receive 1 — better for each than mutual α.

text.fair: If your partner chooses β, β is better for you too: 1 > −1.
text.selfish: If your partner chooses β, α is better for you: 3 > 1.

text.fair: For your partner, α strictly dominates β. So you expect α and respond with α: 0 > −3. Your own α is not strictly dominant.
text.selfish: Your α strictly dominates β. You choose α regardless of your partner’s preferences.

written.title: Explain it in your own words
written.prompt: Why can’t you simply choose β, even if both players understand that (1,1) is better than (0,0)? Explain without quoting a definition.
written.context: You choose the row; your partner chooses the column. Both players care only about their own grade; the matrix shows their payoffs.
written.rubric: A good explanation includes two ideas: choosing β does not make the other player choose β; if your partner chooses β, you personally have an incentive to deviate to α and get 3 instead of 1.

quickAnswer.body: Strict dominance requires a strictly higher payoff for every possible choice of the other player.
